title: Design and analysis of an integrated structure for a spatial camera aluminum alloy mirror based on topology optimization - Scientific Reports
byline: Ren; Jiaqi; Yin; Longhai; Zhang; Wenying; Pei; Zhaohui; Yu; Haoran; Liu; Xiaohan
html:
Abstract

To meet the critical demand for large-aperture, lightweight, and high-surface-accuracy mirrors in thermally stable space cameras, this study proposes a design method for a Φ294 mm aluminum alloy mirror based on topological optimization. First, using (RSA-6061) aluminum alloy as the base material, a topological optimization mathematical model was established by combining the SIMP model with a substructure method. This model uses weighted compliance minimization as the objective function and comprehensively considers axial and lateral gravity loads, polishing load, and thermal load conditions, while adhering to volume fraction constraints. Topological optimization was used to achieve optimal material distribution. Second, the topological optimization contour was used to design the structure with manufacturability considerations, followed by parametric optimization of key dimensions. Finally, finite element simulation and experimental validation were conducted. Simulation results show that the mirror achieved a weight reduction of 72%. Under self-weight in the X, Y, and Z directions, the RMS surface profile accuracy of the primary mirror was 7.02 nm, 7.099 nm, and 2.353 nm, respectively. At a temperature rise of 6 °C, the primary mirror’s surface profile accuracy was 4.571 nm. The fundamental frequency was 360.543 Hz. Experimental verification showed that the RMS surface profile accuracy was 0.0206λ, with a fundamental frequency of 356.78 Hz. All tested metrics met the technical specifications for the space camera.

Introduction

The optical performance of a space camera’s primary mirror plays a decisive role in the camera’s resolution and detection capability1. As space detection accuracy improves, primary mirrors are evolving toward larger apertures, ultra-lightweight designs, and higher surface figure accuracy. This has given rise to three core challenges: payload deformation, manufacturing costs and lead times, and material properties2. Although traditional materials such as silicon carbide and fused quartz possess high specific stiffness, they require lengthy fabrication cycles and entail significantly higher manufacturing costs than metal mirrors3. Furthermore, their thermal expansion mismatch with connecting components makes them susceptible to thermal deformation. Aluminum alloy mirrors, with their low density (2.70 g/cm³), excellent machinability, and good thermal expansion compatibility with connecting components, have emerged as a highly promising solution.

Topological optimization, as a key technology that breaks through the limitations of traditional configurations, has demonstrated significant advantages in the lightweight design of mirrors. Park et al. were among the first to introduce topological optimization into mirror design, they used the root-mean-square (RMS) surface deformation error as the objective function and derived an optimal material distribution configuration under self-weight loading. Liu et al. proposed a lightweight design method for the primary mirror of a large-aperture space telescope based on topological optimization; by optimizing structural compliance subject to volume fraction constraints, they obtained an optimal rib distribution4. Q. Wang et al. employed multi-load topology optimization to design an additively manufactured aluminum mirror structure tailored for single-point diamond turning, and successfully produced a 200 mm-diameter reflector capable of direct infrared imaging5. In addition to compliance-based formulations, Cheng et al. developed a topology optimization framework for mirror supporting structures that directly incorporates Zernike coefficients as the optimization objective, establishing a more direct link between structural topology and optical wavefront performance6.In terms of aperture expansion, the ARIEL mission employs a fully aluminum telescope with a square primary mirror whose major axis measures 1.1 m. Significant weight reduction was achieved through a lightweight honeycomb structure, and parameter optimization was performed with the fundamental frequency-to-mass ratio as the optimization objective, resulting in a surface figure error of 10 nm RMS7. Liu et al. combined topological optimization with parametric design to optimize the telescope’s primary mirror under multiple operating conditions, verifying the feasibility of topological configurations in engineering applications8. Aluminum alloy mirrors offer significant advantages in terms of weight reduction, machinability, and thermal matching. However, due to the more pronounced gravity-induced deformation issues in large-aperture aluminum alloy mirrors9 and the difficulty in achieving high surface accuracy because of the material’s relative softness, they are rarely used in high-resolution detection applications. Research has primarily focused on small-aperture aluminum mirrors10,11,12, with relatively few studies on large-aperture aluminum mirrors.

As the resolution of space cameras improves, there is a growing need for primary mirrors with larger apertures. Researchers have conducted studies on large-aperture aluminum alloy mirrors, focusing on materials, design methods, structure, and manufacturing processes. For example, Yan et al. proposed an integrated design and manufacturing method for aluminum alloy primary mirror assembly, this method combines topology optimization with additive manufacturing to achieve complex structures that are difficult to achieve by mechanical processing13; Newswander et al. conducted a systematic study focused on the heat treatment process for a 500 mm diameter 6061 aluminum alloy primary mirror. Their process route included forging and hot isostatic pressing of the blank, solution heat treatment following rough machining for weight reduction, quenching in an ethylene glycol solution, and ramp quenching, with the aim of effectively eliminating residual stresses14. Weijie Fu et al. focuses on aluminum alloy mirrors with a 500 mm diameter, paying particular attention to material removal rates, residual surface stresses, and the orientation of the machined surface. and employs ultrasonic-assisted grinding to ensure that large-diameter aluminum mirrors meet high manufacturing standards15. P. Picchi et al. studied a large aluminum mirror measuring 1100 mm × 746.9 mm, achieving a surface profile accuracy of SFE ≤ 65 nm RMS after full-diameter final polishing; the heat treatment strategy employed a combination of solution treatment and artificial aging16. Kwijong Park et al.working with Al6061-T6 material, targeted a surface profile accuracy better than λ/8 for a 300-mm-diameter M1 mirror. By comprehensively applying finite element analysis and opto-mechanical integrated analysis methods, and verified the surface profile capability of the primary and secondary mirrors within the support structure in all gravitational directions of a low-temperature (77 K) infrared telescope under T6 solution treatment and artificial aging heat treatment conditions17. Hun Y. L. et al. studied an aluminum hyperbolic mirror of the same aperture (300 mm), employing a self-aligning zero-point lens test system integrated into a fixed tube mount for testing. and successfully verified the optical performance of the mirror and evaluated the effectiveness of the testing method18. The aforementioned research findings provide important references for the manufacturing, heat treatment, and inspection of large-aperture aluminum alloy mirrors.

Beyond conventional machined topologies, bio-inspired optimization strategies combined with additive manufacturing have recently been explored for mirror design, as demonstrated by Chen et al., suggesting further potential for stiffness-to-weight ratio improvement through novel cellular architectures12.To achieve a thermally stable design and reduce the development cost of the primary mirror, this paper takes a Φ294 mm aluminum alloy reflector as the research subject. A multi-objective topological optimization mathematical model incorporating gravity loads, thermal loads, and polishing load was established. Topological optimization was performed on the initial structure, structural features were extracted from the optimization results, and parametric optimization, finite element simulation, and prototype testing were conducted. The integrated design significantly improved stiffness and surface profile control capabilities. Surface figure accuracy testing using a Zygo interferometer revealed an RMS error of 0.0206λ under self-weight, meeting the specified technical requirements. The fundamental frequency was 356.78 Hz, satisfying the system requirement of no less than 200 Hz for the transmission band. This study offers a feasible technical approach and reference for the design of highly lightweight, high-precision aluminum alloy primary mirrors for space cameras.

Technical specifications of the primary mirror

Based on the optical system, the technical parameters and image quality constraints of the primary mirror under various operating conditions were determined to provide input constraints for subsequent topology optimization. The aluminum alloy primary mirror has an effective aperture of Φ290 mm. To account for edge figure degradation during machining, the diameter was increased by 4 mm, resulting in a final diameter of Φ294 mm. Under self-weight conditions, the root mean square (RMS) surface accuracy is required to be ≤ λ/50 (λ = 632.8 nm). Primary mirror material

Common materials for the primary mirror of a space camera include carbon fiber composites, silicon carbide (SiC), microcrystalline glass, single-crystal silicon, and aluminum alloys. Although carbon fiber composites19 offer significant weight-saving advantages.their complex manufacturing processes and high costs mean they are primarily used for primary support structures. Silicon carbide has high stiffness and a low coefficient of thermal expansion, but its production requires stringent conditions, involves long processing cycles, and incurs high development costs. Microcrystalline glass has poor thermal conductivity, is highly sensitive to thermal distortion, and lacks mechanical toughness. Single-crystal silicon is the material of choice for infrared-band loads but suffers from high optical losses in the visible spectrum. In contrast, although aluminum alloys have lower stiffness, they feature mature processing techniques, good thermal dimensional stability, and the ability to be formed as a single integrated piece. Furthermore, with their short manufacturing cycles and low costs, they are better suited for the mass production of aerospace structural components3. Therefore, (RSA-6061) aluminum alloy was selected as the substrate material for the Φ294 mm primary mirror. Topological optimization

Theory of topological optimization

Topology optimization is a design method that uses computational techniques to determine the optimal distribution of material within a defined design space, subject to specified loads and constraints, thereby achieving a balance between performance and weight13. In order to address the trade-off between lightweighting and high surface accuracy in aluminum alloy mirrors, researchers have explored innovative structures under multiple operating conditions23,24 to accommodate actual operating scenarios.

In continuum topological optimization, the Solid Isotropic Material Penalty (SIMP) model is commonly used to describe the relationship between element density and elastic modulus. Its core principle is to use a penalty factor to drive the element density toward either no material or a specific material, which prevents the appearance of a large number of gray elements in the optimization results and simplifies subsequent structural extraction.

During the development of large-aperture aluminum alloy mirrors for space cameras, the mirrors must withstand gravitational loads (e.g., during ground-based machining and testing), transitions to microgravity in orbit, polishing pressure loads during optical machining, and thermal loads caused by ± 6 °C in-orbit temperature fluctuations25.Dong et al. have addressed more realistic orbital thermal environments, including solar radiation and non-uniform temperature distributions, through opto-mechanical-thermal coupling analysis, which could refine the thermal boundary conditions in future work26. Since single-objective optimization cannot simultaneously satisfy surface figure accuracy requirements under multiple operating conditions, a topological optimization approach was developed with weighted compliance minimization as the objective and volume fraction, displacement, and thermal deformation as constraints to achieve optimal material distribution.
